designs.title: Barley and Malt
designs.why: Classic plate structure: the tall ear on the left balances the grain pair on the right, and the four malting stages make a calm baseline. One serif family is used with clear roman caps and italic hierarchy, the labels line up on a shared grid, and the line work is clean and solid at full size. It reads as a plate from 3 m.
designs.fix: Close the dead space under the grain section (between BARLEY GRAIN and the stages row) by moving the grain pair down slightly or enlarging it, so the upper right carries as much weight as the ear.

designs.title: Vitis vinifera
designs.why: The vine engraving is attractive, but the tone is built from a fine 1-px halftone dither, not engraved line, so it will fill in or break up in one-ink screen print. The bottle and glass are crammed into the lower right corner and clash in scale with the plate. The labels float with no leaders, and 'Wine (in bottle and glass)' wraps awkwardly.
designs.fix: Re-render the tone as real line or hatch engraving with no pixel dither, and give the bottle and glass their own band, or drop them, so the vine has room.

designs.title: Fermentation
designs.why: It reads as a textbook figure, not a graphic: a spreadsheet-style line chart, a phases bar and a magnified circle are stacked down the right with no shared rhythm. At full size the bubbles are broken squiggle glyphs, there is a rectangular smudge of dot noise in the wort beside 'Rising CO2 bubbles', and the yeast cells are blobby. There are lots of small labels.
designs.fix: Drop the chart and the phases bar, scale the fermenter cutaway up as the hero with a few labels, and redraw the bubble fill cleanly without the rectangular noise patch.

designs.title: Oak Barrel
designs.why: The top half (elevation plus exploded staves) is a good blueprint composition. The lower half is three near-identical hoop ellipses stacked down the left, which is repetitive and dull. Type is inconsistent: the stave spec block mixes fake small caps with a different numeral face ('75mm' with no space), and the centre line cuts through the bottom 'Ø570 mm' dimension. The hoops are drawn the same size despite labelled diameters of 570 and 690.
designs.fix: Crop to the elevation and exploded view, scale them up to fill the sheet, and reset all labels in one consistent caps style, with dimension text clear of the centre lines.

designs.title: Pot Still
designs.why: A strong, readable silhouette. The swan neck and lyne arm lead the eye in an arc into the worm tub and down to the jug, which is a natural reading path. The engraving is confident and holds up at full size. Labels are a single bold serif with tidy leaders, though some are wordy and 'Cold Water In' / 'Warm Water Out' are set smaller than the rest.
designs.fix: Edit the labels down (drop redundant parentheticals such as '(Cold Water Surrounds)' and '(shows vapour path)') and set every label at one size.

designs.title: Joiner's Tools
designs.why: The best typography of the set: an authentic catalogue system of 'No.' numerals, bold caps names and letterspaced small-caps sizes, applied consistently. The engraved tools have crisp, printable line and a clear rhythm (plane as header, the chisel row, then mallet and dividers). It reads well from distance.
designs.fix: Tighten the bottom row: the brace and saw drift apart and sit lower than the grid above, so align their captions on one baseline and pull them up to match the spacing of the upper rows.

designs.title: Shaping
designs.why: A dramatic, well-composed figure with a good diagonal along the board, but at full size all the mid-tones are a 1-px checkerboard dither, not engraved line, which risks plugging up or moire in screen print. The SHAPING heading is a generic letterspaced grotesque that is small next to the image and does not match its engraved character. The bottom of the image dissolves raggedly.
designs.fix: Rebuild the tone as true line engraving or coarse hatch (no pixel dither), then set a heading in a heavier face that matches the engraving and is scaled to the image width.

designs.title: Motorcycle
designs.why: The workshop-sheet grid is good: the hero side view is framed by lettered detail views, and a typewriter mono is used consistently with a tidy specs table. Up close the drafting falls apart. Dimension lines are broken and dangling (the stray ticks at 72, the floating Ø38 arrows, the fragmented 1980/325 lines), arrowheads are missing, and the engine detail's kickstart is crude. A technical drawing lives or dies on that precision.
designs.fix: Redraw every dimension as a continuous line with proper extension lines and arrowheads, figures centred in gaps, so the drafting looks as exact as the subject.
